title: Queues handle work later
summary: Put slow jobs in a queue and let workers finish them later. Count a growing backlog, then plan acknowledgments, duplicate jobs, and failure handling.
introduction: At a library desk, a learner can leave a request for a printed reading list and collect it later. A queue lets an app keep a similar list of jobs. This helps when work does not need to finish inside the first reply.
learningObjectives: Calculate a backlog from arriving and completed jobs
Plan for duplicate messages and jobs that keep failing

blocks.text: A **producer** adds jobs to a queue. A **worker**, also called a consumer, takes jobs and does the work. The waiting jobs form a **backlog**.

A queue can smooth a short rush and separate slow work from a quick reply. It does not make the work disappear. If jobs arrive faster than workers finish them for a long time, the backlog keeps growing.

After successful work, a worker sends an **acknowledgment**, often shortened to ack. In an at-least-once delivery plan, a job that was not acknowledged may be delivered again. The worker must be safe when a job repeats.

items: Start with no waiting jobs. In each round, 5 new print jobs arrive.
Workers can finish 3 jobs per round.
After the first round, 2 jobs remain. After the second, 4 remain.
After four rounds, 8 jobs are waiting. The queue delays overload; it does not solve this sustained gap.

blocks.text: This small JavaScript model runs in the playground. Its numbers and events are chosen for learning. It does not create servers or measure a real service.

blocks.alt: A book service saves a job in a durable queue. A worker processes the job and acknowledges success.
blocks.caption: A reply that says “queued” does not mean “finished.” A worker can receive the same job again after a failure.

blocks.title: Queues handle work later model
Expected result
blocks.content:
round 1: 2 waiting
round 2: 4 waiting
round 3: 6 waiting
round 4: 8 waiting

blocks.text: This model groups work into rounds. A real queue has different job sizes and delivery times. Monitor the age of the oldest job as well as the job count.
A response such as accepted means the request was durably accepted for processing under the service's rules. It does not mean the print job is finished. Give callers a job ID and a truthful status.

rows: Can clear jobs faster when work can run in parallel
Shared printers or databases may remain the bottleneck
Protects the service during a long overload
Callers need a clear retry or rejection response
Keeps repeatedly failing jobs for inspection
Needs alerts and a safe repair or replay process

blocks.text: Suppose a worker creates the report, then crashes before acknowledging the job. Redelivery can happen. Use a durable job ID and a safe rule that records completion together with the effect where possible.
Multiple workers and retries can change completion order. If order matters for one book or user, choose a suitable grouping and ordering rule. Do not assume every queue provides global order.

items: Change workerCapacity from 3 to 6. Predict the waiting count after each round.
It stays 0 because only 5 jobs arrive each round. The spare capacity is unused in this model, but it may help during a short rush.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not acknowledge a job before its required work is safely complete. A crash afterward could lose work the queue believes was finished.
